messages.subject: Edit Source
parts:
Is it possible for me to edit one of the source functions in my
installation of rattle and then be able to use it? I have tried to
locate the rattle objects but without any luck (seems like I remember
being able to see them a year or so ago). I want to make some small
additions to the GLM and scoring portions to be able to save me some
work. (I want to save the observed values with the predicted values
when doing a gaussian glm, and also run some goodness of fit
analysis.)

So I guess thus boils down to:
1) Can I edit and use the function?
2) Where are they?

Hi Ed,

Sure. You can view any of the source code in R itself either directly
for exported functions (like when you type "rattle") and indirectly
for internal functions (like "rattle:::executeEvaluateScore"). All
source code is also available at
http://code.google.com/p/rattle/source.

A quick way to do what you want is to grab all the source code, put it
into a directory (e.g., "/home/fred/rattle/"), and source all of the files
into R with:

> loc <- "/home/fred/rattle/"
> lapply(paste(loc, grep(".*\\.R$", dir(loc), value=TRUE), sep=""), source)

Then edit whichever files you want, and rerun the lapply command (to
reload your new code).

Also, send me any changes you make as they will probably be useful to
incorporate directly into Rattle for others to use also.

For the "save the observed values with the predicted values when doing
a gaussian glm" I would think a button in the Model tab called Save
Predicted might be useful, with similar functionality to the "Score"
radio button on the Evaluate tab, and modelled on the function
executeEvaluateScore (in rattle.R).

For the "goodness of fit analysis" I'd add that into the Evaluate
tab.

In both cases, its easy for me to update the GUI if I have sample R
code that implements the functionality you want underneath.

Regards,
Graham

OK, Here is some code I can pass along that allows the Correlation
Cluster Dendrogram to handle much longer variable names by modifying
the right margin. It also makes the font smaller when there are many
variables. It probably could use more testing but seems to work fine
for me.

File: rattle.R (function: executeExploreHiercor)
## Construct the commands.

cor.cmd <- sprintf('cc <- cor(%s, use="pairwise")', dataset)
hclust.cmd <- 'hc <- hclust(dist(cc), "ave")'
dend.cmd <- "dn <- as.dendrogram(hc)"

#Modification by Ed Cox to increase margin for long variable names.
fontsize <- .75
if (ncols>45) {fontsize <- .60}
labwidth <-
eval(parse(text=sprintf('max(as.vector(lapply(colnames(%s),"nchar"),mode="integer"))
+2', dataset)))
plot.cmd <- paste('op <- par(mar = c(3,4,3,',labwidth/3.5,')) ',
'plot(dn, horiz=TRUE, ',
'nodePar=list(col=3:2, cex=c(2.0, 0.75), pch=
21:22, ',
'bg= c("light blue", "pink"), ',
'lab.cex = ',fontsize,', lab.col = "tomato"), ',
'edgePar=list(col="gray", lwd=2)',
') ',
genPlotTitleCmd("Variable Correlation Clusters",
crs$dataname),' ',
'par(op) ',
sep="")

## Start logging and executing the R code.

messages.subject: Re: Edit Source
parts:
Here is a mod that adds a plot to Evaluate to show predicted values
against observed with a pseudo-R-square. The code seems to work well,
but does NOT include provision to also output to the log.

File: rattle.R (function: getSelectedVariables)
## And finally, remove the na.omit if there is one, replacing it
## with specifically removing just the rows that were removed in
## the predict command.

if (not.null(omitted))
scoreset = sub(")", "[-omitted,]", sub("na.omit\\(", "",
scoreset))
obsset <- scoreset #**********Save copy for mod referred to
below************
scoreset <- sprintf('subset(%s, select=c(%s))',
scoreset,
ifelse(is.null(idents), "",
sprintf('"%s"', paste(idents,
collapse='", "'))))
appendLog("Extract the corresponding identifier fields from the
dataset.",
sprintf("scores <- %s", scoreset))

scores <- eval(parse(text=scoreset))

#Modification by Ed Cox to plot predictions vs. observed values
obsset <- sprintf('subset(%s, select=crs$target)',obsset)
obs <- eval(parse(text=obsset))
fitpoints <- cbind(obs,Predicted=crs$pr)
fitcorr <- format(cor(fitpoints[,1],fitpoints[,2]),digits=4)
op <- par(c(lty="solid",col="blue"))
plot(fitpoints,asp=1,main="Predicted vs.
Observed",sub=paste("Pseudo R-square = ",fitcorr))
prline <- lm(fitpoints[,2]~fitpoints[,1])
abline(prline)
par(c(lty="dashed",col="black"))
abline(0,1) #add a diagonal representing perfect correlation.
legend("topleft",legend=c("Best Fit to Points","Ideal
Regression"),
lty=c(1,2),col=c("blue","black"),bty="n" )
par(op)
#End Mod

appendLog("Write the scores to file.",
paste('write.csv(cbind(scores, predict=crs$pr), file="',
score.file, '", row.names=FALSE)', sep=""))

write.csv(cbind(scores, predict=crs$pr), file=score.file,
row.names=FALSE)

infoDialog("The scores for", mtype, "have been saved into the
file",
paste(getwd(), score.file, sep="/"))

messages.subject: Re: Edit Source
parts:
I ran across a bug and managed a quick fix, but I know it is only a
band-aid that is not a general solution. In function:
executeEvaluateScore I made the change shown below. The issue appears
to be that it complains if there are no NAs to remove so I bypass the
omission code. I know this is not a general fix because I know I ran
into a case where it failed, but maybe you will have the insight as to
what the real problem is and can do it right.

(PS: The project I was working on was very well received and it looks
there is more work coming in the near future!!! Rattle ROCKS!)

## First deal with the na.omit case, to capture the list of rows
## omitted.

#Mod by Ed Cox to fix error when no NAs in test set
scorevarlist <-
c(getSelectedVariables("ident"),getSelectedVariables("target"),getSelectedVariables("input"),getSelectedVariables("risk"))
tmpset <- crs$dataset[-crs$sample, scorevarlist]
if (substr(scoreset, 1, 7) == "na.omit" & !dim(tmpset)
[1]==dim(na.omit(tmpset))[1] )
{
omit.cmd <- paste("omitted <- ", scoreset, "@na.action", sep="")
appendLog("Record rows omitted from predict command.", omit.cmd)
eval(parse(text=omit.cmd))
}
else
omitted <- NULL

the axis ranges which is not necessarily true when doing linear
regression (which is where this chart is useful).

- Ed
